parts.problemMd:
A random variable has distribution $B(n,p)$. Anna uses a single observation of the random variable to carry out a hypothesis test.

Write down the conditions that must be met in order to model a random variable using the binomial distribution.
Explain how the parameters $n$ and $p$ are used in the context of a hypothesis test.
Anna is carrying out a two-tailed hypothesis test. Explain how what is being tested for in a two-tailed test differs from what is being tested for in a one-tailed test.

For the random variable $X \text{tilde} B ( 20 , 0.3 )$ calculate

(i) $P(X\leq2)$

(ii) $P(X<3)$

A hypothesis test is to be carried out using an observation of the random variable $X$ to test the hypotheses:

`H _ 0 ∶ p = 0.3 H _ 1 ∶ p less than 0.3`

Before carrying out the test, a significance level of 5% is chosen. The critical region is defined as $X\leq2.$

(i) Explain why the critical region is defined as $X\leq2$.

(ii) State the actual significance level for the test.

Alina is running for student council president at her school.  She claims she has the support of 60% of students in the school.  A rival candidate, John, wants to test at the 10% level of significance whether Alina is overestimating her support.

In mathematical terms, the experiment John conducts uses an observation of the random variable  $X \text{tilde} B ( 100 , p )$to test the hypotheses:

`H _ 0 ∶ p = 0.6 H _ 1 ∶ p less than 0.6`

(i) State how many people are in John’s sample and explain what the parameter $p$ means in the context of this question.

(ii) Explain why John has chosen this alternative hypothesis for his test.

Assuming Alina’s claim is true, John calculates the following cumulative probabilities:

| $x$ | 51 | 52 | 53 | 54 | 55 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $P(X\leqx)$ | 0.04230 | 0.06379 | 0.09298 | 0.13109 | 0.17890 |

In John’s survey, 55 people say that they will support Alina.

(i) Calculate $P(X=55)$.

(ii) State whether John should compare the value of $P(X\leq55)$ or  $P(X=55)$ with his significance level of 10%.

(iii) In the context of this question, write a conclusion for John’s test.
Write down the critical value and the critical region for John’s test.

A hypothesis test at the 6% significance level is carried out on a coin using the following hypotheses:

`H _ 0 ∶ p = 1 half H _ 1 colon p != 1 half`

(i) Give an example of what the parameter, $p$, could represent.

(ii) In the context of your answer from part (i), explain what is meant by $p=\frac{1}{2}$.

(iii) This is a two-tailed test. Explain what should be done with the 6% significance level.

A single observation $x$ is to be taken from a binomial distribution $X \text{tilde} B ( 100 , p )$ to test the hypotheses for the coin. One tail of the critical region is found to be  $X\leq6$.

(i) Using your knowledge of the binomial distribution $B(100,0.5)$, write down the other tail of the critical region.

(ii) Write down the set of values for $x$ which would lead to the acceptance of the null hypothesis.

In a school where all the teachers drink coffee in the staffroom, a headteacher wants to see if using a new brand of coffee in the staffroom improves teachers’ report writing punctuality.  Previously, 75% of teachers in her school would meet the deadline for writing reports.  After the new brand of coffee is introduced the headteacher takes a random sample of 15 teachers, and conducts an experiment to test whether the proportion of teachers meeting the deadline on the next set of reports has improved.  The test is conducted at the 5% significance level, using the following hypotheses:

`H _ 0 ∶ p = 0.75 H _ 1 ∶ p greater than 0.75`

(i) Write down a suitable distribution for the random variable $X$, the number of teachers in the headteacher’s sample who meet the deadline.

(ii) Calculate the probability that all the teachers in the sample would meet the deadline if the null hypothesis were true.

(iii) By first calculating the probability that exactly 14 of the teachers would meet the deadline if the null hypothesis were true, find the critical value for the test.

A study of ladybirds in the UK found that 65% of all ladybirds are found to be of the seven-spot species.  Alex believes that more than 65% of the ladybirds in his garden are of the seven-spot species.  He conducts a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level by collecting a sample of 25 ladybirds from his garden and counting the number of them that are seven-spot ladybirds.

(i) Alex uses the random variable $X \sim B \left(n , p\right)$ to represent the number of seven-spot ladybirds in his sample.  Explain what $n$ and $p$ represent in the context of Alex’ experiment.

(ii) State an assumption Alex has made in order to use the distribution in part (a)(i).

(iii) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses that Alex could use to test his belief that more than 65% of the ladybirds in his garden are seven-spot ladybirds.

Alex finds that 21 out of the 25 ladybirds in his sample are seven-spot ladybirds.

(i) The $p$-value for the observed test statistic is 0.03205. Write this in the form  $P(X\geqa)=b.$ .

(ii) Alex has not yet calculated the critical value for his hypothesis test.  Explain why he does not need to do this to come to a conclusion for his test.

The probability of a student in a primary school library returning his or her books on time had been found to be 0.35.  Joanna, the school librarian, has started a new incentive scheme and believes that more students are now returning their books on time because of it.  She conducts a hypothesis test using the null hypothesis  $H_{0}:p=0.35$ to test her belief

(i) State a suitable alternative hypothesis to test Joanna’s belief that more students are now returning their books on time.

(ii) Write down the conditions under which Joanna could use a binomial probability distribution to model this problem.

Joanna takes a random sample of 30 students who have checked out books and finds that under the new incentive scheme 15 of them return their books on time.  She calculates the following probabilities for the random variable  $X \text{tilde} B ( 30 , 0.35 )$ :

$P(X=14)=0.06112$

$P(X=15)=0.03511$

$P(X\geq16)=0.03008$

Write down the values of $P(X\geq15)$ and  $P(X\geq14).$

Write a conclusion for the hypothesis test, in context, if Joanna had chosen a significance level of:

(i) 5%

(ii) 10%

The number of leaves on the grass in Danny’s garden on October 1<sup>st</sup> every year has a Poisson distribution with mean 280.

Given that Danny’s garden is 56 square metres,

(i) Write down the distribution for the number of leaves per square metre in Danny’s garden on October 1<sup>st</sup>,

(ii) Find the probability that in a randomly chosen square metre of Danny’s garden, there are less than 3 leaves.

Danny’s neighbour has cut down a tree and Danny believes this will decrease the number of leaves in his garden this year. He is devising a hypothesis test to test his theory at the 10% significance level. On October 1<sup>st</sup> he will choose a square metre of his garden at random and count the number of leaves.

Write down suitable null and alternative hypotheses Danny can use for his test.
Use your answer to part (a)(ii) to determine if finding 2 leaves will lead Danny to accept or reject his null hypothesis. Justify your answer.
Determine the critical region for this hypothesis test and hence, write down the maximum number of leaves that will lead Danny to reject his null hypothesis.

A company releases a rapid testing kit for a particular virus and claims that the kit is correct 90% of the time. A medical professional believes this is false advertising and carries out a hypothesis test at the 1% significance level to test the company’s claim.

For each of the following statements, write down whether the hypothesis test has resulted in an error, and if so state whether it is a Type I or a Type II error.

(i) The kit is correct 85% of the time. The medical professional rejects the null hypothesis in favour of the alternative hypothesis.

(ii) The kit is correct 95% of the time. The medical professional accepts the null hypothesis.

(iii) The kit is correct 90% of the time. The medical professional rejects the null hypothesis in favour of the alternative hypothesis.

(iv) The kit is correct 90% of the time. The medical professional accepts the null hypothesis.
Write down the greatest possible probability of the hypothesis test resulting in a Type I error.

A single observation is taken from a discrete random variable $X \text{tilde} B ( 15 , 0.4 )$  to test $H_{0}:p=0.4$ against $H_{1}:p<0.4$.

Using a 5% level of significance, find the critical region for this test.

The actual value for the observation was 4.

State a conclusion to the hypothesis test for this value, giving a reason for your answer.

Harry is using the random variable $X \text{tilde} B ( 40 , 0.15 )$  to test the hypotheses:

$H_{0}:p=0.15$

$H_{1}:p\neq0.15$

Harry states that the critical regions are $X\leq2$ and $X\geq11$.

(i) Given that $P(X\geq11)=0.029921$, calculate the probability of incorrectly rejecting the null hypothesis.

(ii) State which type of error is represented in part (a)(i).

(iii) State, with a reason, the conclusion of Harry’s test given that the observed value is $x=10$.

Sally is using the random variable $Y \text{tilde} B ( 35 , 0.03 )$ to test the hypotheses:

$H_{0}:p=0.3$

$H_{1}:p>0.3$

Sally observes the value $y=3$.

(i) Find the relevant probability that Sally should calculate to test her hypothesis using the observed value.

(ii) State, with a reason, the conclusion of Sally’s test if a 5% level of significance is used.

Charlie, the owner of a chocolate shop, claims that more than 60% of people can tell the difference between two brands of chocolate.  Charlie takes a random sample of 15 customers and asks them to taste both brands of chocolate.  He records that 12 of them could successfully tell the difference between the two brands of chocolate.

State suitable null and alternative hypotheses to test Charlie’s claim.
Test, at the 10% level of significance, whether Charlie’s claim is justified.

Nationally it is reported that four out of five people are right-handed.  Edward, an education researcher, takes a random sample of 30 children under the age of 18 years old and records the number of them, $X$, who write with their right hand.

Assuming that the national proportion applies to the sample, write down a suitable distribution for $X$.

Edward believes that the proportion of right-handed children differs from the national proportion for all people. To test his belief, he uses his sample of 30 children.

State suitable null and alternative hypotheses to test Edward’s belief.

Given that $P(X\leq19)=0.02561625\mathrm{and}P(X\leq20)=0.06108714$, find the critical values for a two-tailed test at the 10% significance level for Edward’s belief.  You should state the probability of rejection for each tail, which should be less than 0.05 for each.
Use your critical values to find the probability of the test resulting in a Type I error.

Out of the 30 children in the sample, Edward recorded that 20 of them write with their right hand.

Comment on Edward’s belief based on this observation.

The existing treatment for a disease is known to be effective in 85% of cases. Dr Sabir develops a new treatment which she claims is more effective than the existing one. To test her claim she uses the new treatment on a sample of 60 patients with the disease and uses a binomial distribution to model the number of them who are cured.

Explain two assumptions that Dr Sabir has made when using a binomial distribution to model the number of patients cured by the new treatment.

Dr Sabir notes that her treatment was effective for 57 out of the 60 patients used in the sample.

Test, at the 1% level of significance, the validity of Dr Sabir’s claim that her treatment is more effective than the existing one. State your hypotheses clearly.
State the conclusion you would have reached if a 5% level of significance had been used for this test.

The owner of a website claims that his website receives an average of 60 hits per hour. An interested purchaser believes the website receives on average less than 60 hits per hour. The owner chooses a 10 minute period and observes that the website receives 4 hits. Assuming that the number of hits the website receives follows a Poisson Distribution,

(i) State null and alternative hypotheses to test the purchaser’s claim, and

(ii) Test at the 1% significance level whether the purchaser’s claim is justified.

A “double yolker” is an egg which contains two yolks. It is known that the probability of a chicken laying a double yolker is 0.1%. A chicken farmer, Paolo, claims that double yolkers are rarer than the stated 0.1%. To test his claim, Paolo records that his chickens lay 1217 eggs in a month and he uses these as his sample. He discovers that none of these eggs are double yolkers.

Test, at the 5% level of significance, whether there is evidence to support Paolo’s claim that double yolkers are rarer than 0.1%. State your hypotheses clearly.

Paolo decides to take a larger sample so extends his test to six months. During this time, a sample of 7300 eggs is formed and two of them are double yolkers.

Use a suitable approximation to show that there is evidence, at the 5% level of significance, to support Paolo’s claim that double yolkers are rarer than 0.1%.
Paolo concludes that the probability of a double yolker is **definitely** less than 0.1%. Give a reason to explain whether Paolo’s conclusion is justified.

It is known that 61% of male dragons eat more than 20 sheep within a day. Bill, a dragon breeder, suspects that the proportion of female dragons that eat more than 20 sheep within a day is different to males.

State suitable null and alternative hypotheses for a two-tailed test for Bill’s suspicion.

To test his suspicion, Bill observes a random sample of 18 female dragons during a full day and counts how many sheep they eat. He finds that 15 out of the 18 female dragons ate more than 20 sheep within the day.

Test, at the 5% level, whether there is evidence to support Bill’s suspicion.

Determine the outcome of the test, at the 5% level, if Bill had used a one-tailed test to check whether the proportion of females eating more than 20 sheep within a day is greater than the proportion of males.

Zien and her younger sister Ying are playing a game of ‘rock, paper, scissors’. Zien claims that she can predict which out of the three options – rock, paper or scissors – Ying will choose every time they play the game. Ying thinks Zien is just guessing so she decides to conduct a hypothesis test to test Zien’s claim. They play the game 10 times and if Zien is correct in 8 or more games, Ying agrees to accept Zien’s claim.

State suitable null and alternative hypotheses for Ying’s test.
Calculate the probability of a Type I error.
Find the range of values that Ying could have been using for the significance level of her test, and hence write down the most likely significance level she used.

Historical records show that England wins 45% of Ashes test cricket series.  Rory believes that in the recent past that proportion has decreased.  To test this, he looks at their results in the last 17 series.

Using a 5% level of significance identify the critical region to enable Rory to test his claim.
England have won five series in the last 17. Use your answer in part (a) to state, with a reason, whether this sample supports Rory’s claim.
State an assumption made when using a binomial model.

It is known that there is a 0.35% chance of picking up a virus when downloading a file from a particular website.  After a security update, a security analyst believes that the chances of picking up a virus have been reduced.  In a sample of 1542 files downloaded from the website, 1 virus is detected.  The analyst wishes to use a hypothesis test with significance levels  appropriately chosen to allow her to report with as much certainty as possible that her belief is correct.

Test at the 1%, 5% and 10% significance levels and explain which of those significance levels the analyst should use for the test in her report.

At a school it is known that 80% of students obtain 3 or more A* to C grades in their A levels.  The principal claims that another local school has a different proportion of A* to C grades at A level.

Last year the other school had 57 out of 80 students achieve 3 or more A* to C grades at A level.

Using a two-tailed hypothesis test, test the principal’s claim at the 5% significance level stating suitable null and alternative hypotheses.
Suggest a hypothesis test with an alternative significance level that would lead to a different conclusion.

On a particular Pokémon game, it is possible to create offspring through breeding.  Sometimes when two Pokémon are bred together, their offspring possess a hidden ability.

One Pokémon fan website,$A$, claims that the probability of producing offspring with a hidden ability is 0.6.  Another website,$B$, claims the probability is higher.

Maya conducts an experiment and finds that 17 out of 20 of her Pokémon’s offspring possess a hidden ability.

Use Maya’s sample to test the claim of website  $A$ against website $B$ at the 5% significance level, stating your null and alternative hypotheses clearly.

Website $B$ claims that the probability is 0.8.

Using a two-tailed hypothesis test, test the claim at the 5% significance level and make a statement about which website is more likely to be correct.

The critical regions of a two-tailed hypothesis test to test $B's$ claim are $X\leq12\mathrm{and}X\geq20$. Given that under the null hypothesis $P(X\geq12)=0.990018$, find the probability of the hypothesis test resulting in a Type I error.

A walk-in vaccination centre can model the number of people arriving every 5 minutes by the random variable $X$ with distribution $Po(0.6)$.

State two assumptions required for the Poisson model to be valid.

The centre launches a new advertising campaign and conducts a hypothesis test to see if it has increased the number of people arriving for a vaccine. They choose a half hour period at random and find that 7 people arrive for a vaccine during that time.

Clearly stating your hypotheses, test at the 10% significance level whether the number of arrivals has increased.
Find the probability of a Type I error, being sure to justify your answer.

It is known that in the past customers have had a 90% success rate when attempting to order festival tickets from a particular website. The website manager has made some improvements and claims that its customers should now have a greater probability of success. It is decided to conduct a hypothesis test at the 10% significance level to test the manager’s claim, using the next 50 people who attempt to purchase tickets as a sample.

State the null and alternative hypotheses to be used in conducting the test.

Explain, in context, what is meant by

(i) A Type I error,

(ii) A Type II error.
Find the probability of the hypothesis test resulting in a Type I error.

Out of the next 50 people who attempt to purchase tickets, 48 are successful.

Using the hypotheses from part (a), carry out the appropriate hypothesis test to test the manager’s claim at the 10% significance level.
If after the improvements were made to the website the success rate had in fact become 95%, determine the probability that the hypothesis test could have resulted in a Type II error.

Anna likes to make crocheted fish for her friends.  Anna models the number of faults in her crocheted fish as having a Poisson distribution with a mean of 45 faults per square metre of material.  After taking a course she believes that this rate has decreased, and she decides to test her belief at the 10% significance level by counting the number of errors in a randomly chosen crocheted fish.

One of Anna’s crocheted fish uses 1000 cm<sup>2</sup><sub> </sub>of crocheted material.

State what is meant by a Type I error in the context of the question and find the probability that Anna’s test will result in a Type I error.
Given that Anna finds 2 faults in the randomly chosen crocheted fish, carry out the hypothesis test.
Find the probability that a Type II error could have occurred in Anna’s test, if the rate of faults after Anna took her course has actually become 25 faults per square metre.

A single observation, $x$, is taken from a discrete random variable $X \text{tilde} B ( 15 , p )$ to test `H _ 0 ∶ p = 0.5` against  `H _ 1 ∶ p != 0.5`.

For the purposes of this test, one of the critical regions is specified as being $X\geq12$.

Calculate the probability of incorrectly rejecting the null hypothesis when conducting this test and state whether this would be a Type I or a Type II error.

The probability of a wild Asian elephant living past 40 years old is 45%.

Rosie, a zoologist, obtains data on 20 elephants in captivity and records their ages at death. She suspects that the proportion of Asian elephants that live past 40 years old is smaller for those in captivity than those in the wild.

Using a 1% level of significance, find the critical value of a one-tailed hypothesis test to enable Rosie to test her suspicion. Clearly state your hypotheses.

Rosie finds that only one elephant, out of the 20 in captivity, lived past 40 years old.

(i) Write down the conclusion of the hypothesis test based on this information.

(ii) Calculate the probability that this observed result has led to a Type I error.

Roger’s bunnies are well trained and almost always leave their droppings in a designated area, however, Roger occasionally finds that they have left their droppings in his garden too.

Given that over a six-hour period the probability there are no droppings found in the garden is $4.53999\times10^{-5}$ correct to 6 significant figures, find the mean number of droppings left per hour in Roger’s garden.

Roger’s bunnies’ new treat craze is popcorn and Roger believes that the bunnies leave less droppings in the garden after he has given them this treat. Roger decides to test his theory by giving his bunnies the popcorn and then seeing how many droppings are left in the garden over a three-hour period.

Given that the probability of a Type I error is 0.0404277 correct to 6 significant figures, find the critical region for Roger’s hypothesis test.
Roger finds that two droppings were left in his garden during the three-hour period. Stating your hypotheses clearly, write down the conclusion of Roger’s hypothesis test.

Historic company data shows that the proportion of customers ordering a large vegetable box from Lakebridge Organics* *is 0.4.

Last week a random sample of 12 customers’ orders was taken and it was found that 10 of them had ordered a large vegetable box.

Test, at the 5% significance level, whether this suggests that the proportion of customers ordering large vegetable boxes has increased. State your hypotheses clearly.

Historic company data shows that the proportion of customers ordering a medium vegetable box is also 0.4. Lucinda, a delivery driver, suspects that the proportion of current customers ordering medium boxes is different from 0.4. She takes a random sample of 10 customers’ orders.

(i) Stating your hypotheses clearly, identify the critical regions for a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level.

(ii) State the probability of making a Type I error.
In actual fact, half of all customers order a medium vegetable box when they shop at Lakebridge Organics. Find the probability of the hypothesis test resulting in a Type II error.

A football team, Dinamo Galacticos*, *are trying to decide on a colour for their new kit.  They are told by a local sports commentator that the proportion of games won by teams wearing red is 0.6.  The manager takes a random sample of  games where one team wears red and observes how many are won by the team wearing red.  Assuming that the proportion of games won by teams in red really is 0.6, then the probability that all of the games would be won is equal to 0.0279936.

Find the value of $n$.

The manager decides to increase her random sample to include $n+4$ games. She suspects that the actual proportion of games won by teams in red is lower than 0.6.

(i) Using a 5% level of significance, find the critical region for a one-tailed hypothesis test. State your hypotheses clearly.

(ii) Describe, in context, what a Type I error would be and find the probability the test results in a Type I error.

(iii) Using a 10% level of significance, find the largest number of games that could be won by teams wearing red without the test resulting in a possible Type II error.

The sports commentator later says that he may have gotten mixed up, and that he thinks it is actually teams wearing green that win 60% of their games.

Given that teams wearing green have won 13 games from the last 15 in which they played, test at the 5% significance level whether the commentator’s new claim is justified. You must clearly state your null and alternative hypotheses.

A catering company’s past records show that the proportion of their customers who are vegetarian has previously been 0.2.  The company decides to take a random sample of 30 current customers to test whether that figure 0.2 is still valid for their current customer base.

Let $X$ denote the number of vegetarians in the sample. Given that, if there has been no change to the proportion of customers who are vegetarian, the probability that less than 10 customers are vegetarian is 0.938913 correct to 6 decimal places, find the probability of the test resulting in a Type I error, using a 10% significance level.

The number of vegetarian customers in the sample is 11.  One of the company’s employees used the same sample to suggest that this shows that the proportion of vegetarian customers has not just changed but has in fact increased.

Use this observed value to test, at the 5% level of significance, whether the proportion of vegetarian customers has increased. State your hypotheses clearly.

Given that the proportion of vegetarian customers is in fact 0.25 and that the probability that less than 10 customers are vegetarian is actually 0.803407 correct to 6 decimal places, find the probability that the test in part (a) produces a Type II error.

A random variable has distribution  $X \text{tilde} B ( 20 , p )$.

In order to test the hypotheses

`H _ 0 ∶ p = 0.4 H _ 1 ∶ p != 0.4`

a random observation of $X$ is taken and found to be 3.

Carry out a hypothesis test at the 2% significance level.

Another random variable has distribution  $Y \text{tilde} B ( m , p )$.

A random observation of is taken and found to be 0. Using the same hypotheses as above, find the maximum value of $m$ for which $H_{0}$ would not be rejected at the 2% significance level.

Another random observation of $Y$ is taken and found to be $y$. For the same hypotheses as above, this provides evidence to reject $H_{0}$ at the 5% significance level.

Using your answer to part (b) as the value for $m$, find the possible values of $y$.

A random sample of 25 independent observations of the random variable $X \text{tilde} N ( 50 , 10 ² )$ is taken. The sample mean, $̅X$ is calculated.

Explain why `̅ X tilde N ( 50 , 2 ^2 )`.

Find the value of $k$ such that:

(i) $P(̅X<k)=0.05$

(ii) $P(̅X>k)=0.1$

The random variable $S$ follows a normal distribution with a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 8.  The mean of 16 independent observations of $S$ is denoted as $\overline{S}$.

Explain why the standard deviation of $\overline{S}$ is 2.

By standardising and using the table of values for the normal distribution, find:

(i) $P(S<39)$

(ii) $P(\overline{S}<39)$

By standardising and using the table of critical values for the normal distribution, find:

(i) the value of $x$ such that $P(S>x)=0.1$

(ii) the value of $y$ such that $P(\overline{S}>y)=0.1$.

The population mean of the random variable $X \text{tilde} N ( mu , 6 ^{2} )$  is being tested using a null hypothesis $H_{0}:μ=15$ against the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}:μ<15.$ A random sample of 10 observations is taken from the population and the sample mean is calculated as $\overline{x}$.

(i) Write down the distribution of the sample mean,$\overline{X}$.

(ii) Find the test statistic, $z$, for $̅x=12$ and hence find $P(̅X<12)$.

(iii) Find the rejection region for $̅X$, when a 10% significance level is used.

The population mean of the random variable $Y \text{tilde} N ( mu , 10 )$ is being tested using a null hypothesis $H_{0}:μ=0$ against an alternative hypothesis.  A random sample of 36 observations is taken from the population and the critical region for the test is $\overline{Y}>0.7778$.

(I) Write down the appropriate alternative hypothesis for the test.

(ii) Write down the distribution of the sample mean, $\overline{Y}$.

(iii) Find the level of significance that was used in the test.

A random sample of size 100 is taken from a population given by $X \text{tilde} N ( mu , 9 )$.

A two-tailed test is used to investigate the null hypothesis $H_{0}:μ=50$ at the 10% level of significance.

(i) Write down a suitable alternative hypothesis for this test.

(ii) Find the rejection regions for $\overline{X}$ for this test.
Given that there is insufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis when $\overline{x}=k,$ write down an inequality for the range of values of $k.$

Write suitable null and alternative hypotheses for each of the following situations.

(i) A butcher advertises that their burgers weigh 180 g.  A customer believes that the burgers are on average underweight.

(ii) The CEO of a large multi-academy trust claims that the students in her schools spend on average 150 minutes on homework each night.  A parent wants to test if the claim is true, so he takes a random sample of 20 students and calculates the mean time spent on homework during a specific night.

(iii) The average weight of an adult male in the UK was known to be 83.6 kg before the country had a lockdown.  After the lockdown ended the standard deviation of weights remained the same.  A fitness instructor is investigating whether adult males in the UK got heavier during the lockdown.

(iv) The manager of a company buys a hot drink vending machine for his employees.  The machine is supposed to dispense 350 ml of coffee when a customer selects the medium option.  The manager believes that the machine does not dispense enough coffee.  To test this, he takes a sample of 25 medium coffees and calculates the mean as 342 ml.

The Starlighter is a new brand of flashlight.  It is known that the brightness, $B$ lumens, of the light emitted from a Starlighter follows a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 15 lumens.  Annie, a salesperson, claims that the mean brightness of a Starlighter is greater than 110 lumens.  To test her claim, the null hypothesis `H _ 0 ∶ mu = 110` is used with a 5% level of significance.

Write down a suitable alternative hypothesis to test Annie’s claim.

To test Annie’s claim a random sample of 40 Starlighters is taken and the mean brightness, $\overline{b}$, is calculated.

(i) Assuming that the null hypothesis is true write down the distribution of the sample mean, $\overline{B}$.

(ii) Find the critical region for the test.

Given that the mean of sample is $\overline{b}=114.5$lumens,

(i) State whether there is sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis at the 5% level of significance

(ii) Write a conclusion, in context, to the test.

The wingspan of a small white butterfly, $W$ cm, follows a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 0.8 cm.  A report states that the average wingspan of a small white butterfly is 4.1 cm.  Kenzie, a butterfly enthusiast, wants to conduct a two-tailed hypothesis test, using a 5% level of significance, to investigate the validity of the statement made by the report.

(i) Write down a suitable null hypothesis for Kenzie’s test.

(ii) Write down a suitable alternative hypothesis for Kenzie’s test.

Kenzie uses a random sample of 6 small white butterflies and finds that the mean wingspan is 2.65 cm.  Kenzie starts off the hypothesis test as follows:

$I f H_{0} i s t r u e t h e n W \text{tilde} N ( 4.1 , 0.8 ^{2} )$

$P(W<2.65)=P(Z<-1.8125)\,=1-0.9651\,=0.0349<0.05$

Identify and explain the two mistakes that Kenzie has made in his hypothesis test.

(i) Find the test statistic, $z$, that Kenzie should use.

parts.solutionMd:
(i)

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $λ = 5$ and $r = 4$

$\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \text{e}^{-5} \frac{5^{4}}{4!}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = 0 . 175467 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = 0 . 175$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

$X \leq 2$ means $X = 0 ,  1 \text{or} 2$, so add those three terms

$\text{P} ( X \leq 2 ) = \text{P} ( X = 0 ) + \text{P} ( X = 1 ) + \text{P} ( X = 2 )$

$\text{P} ( X \leq 2 ) = \text{e}^{-5} \frac{5^{0}}{0!} + \text{e}^{-5} \frac{5^{1}}{1!} + \text{e}^{-5} \frac{5^{2}}{2!}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X \leq 2 ) = 0 . 124652 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \leq 2 ) = 0 . 125$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(iii)

$X \geq 2$ is every outcome except $X = 0$ and $X = 1$, so subtract those two terms from 1

$\text{P} ( X \geq 2 ) = 1 - \text{P} ( X \leq 1 )$

`\text{P}(X \geq 2) = 1 - \left(\text{e}^{-5}\dfrac{5^{0}}{0!} + \text{e}^{-5}\dfrac{5^{1}}{1!}\right)`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X \geq 2 ) = 0 . 959572 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \geq 2 ) = 0 . 960$** (3 s.f.)**

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $λ = 3$ and $r = 5$

$\text{P} ( X = 5 ) = \text{e}^{-3} \frac{3^{5}}{5!}$

**[M1]**

Simplify the fraction, since $3^{5} = 243$ and $5 ! = 120$

$\frac{3^{5}}{5!} = \frac{243}{120} = \frac{81}{40}$

$\text{P} ( X = 5 ) = \frac{81}{40} \text{e}^{-3}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

$X \leq 1$ means $X = 0$ or $X = 1$, so add those two terms

$\text{P} ( X \leq 1 ) = \text{e}^{-3} \frac{3^{0}}{0!} + \text{e}^{-3} \frac{3^{1}}{1!}$

**[M1]**

Use $3^{0} = 1$ and $0 ! = 1 ! = 1$

$\text{P} ( X \leq 1 ) = \text{e}^{-3} + 3 \text{e}^{-3}$

$\text{P} ( X \leq 1 ) = 4 \text{e}^{-3}$

**[A1]**

(iii)

$X \geq 2$ is every outcome except $X \leq 1$, so subtract the answer to (ii) from 1

$\text{P} ( X \geq 2 ) = 1 - \text{P} ( X \leq 1 )$

$\text{P} ( X \geq 2 ) = 1 - 4 \text{e}^{-3}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct expression for P(X = 5), $\text{e}^{-3} \frac{3^{5}}{5!}$.
> 
> **A1**: P(X = 5) = $\frac{81}{40} \text{e}^{-3}$, or an exact equivalent such as $2 . 025 \text{e}^{-3}$ or $\frac{243}{120} \text{e}^{-3}$.
> 
> **M1**: P(0) + P(1), with both terms correct. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: P(X ≤ 1) = $4 \text{e}^{-3}$.
> 
> **B1**: P(X ≥ 2) = $1 - 4 \text{e}^{-3}$. Follow through 1 minus your answer to (ii).
> 
> The answers must be exact, in terms of e. A decimal answer alone (0.101, 0.199, 0.801) does not earn the final mark for that sub-part.

parts.problemMd:

(ii) $λ = 2 . 5$

(iii) $λ = 0 . 01$

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $r = 0$; since $λ^{0} = 1$ and $0 ! = 1$, this is just $\text{e}^{-λ}$

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{0}}{0!} = \text{e}^{-λ}$

(i)

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \text{e}^{-7} = 0 . 000911882 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = 0 . 000912$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(ii)

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \text{e}^{-2.5} = 0 . 0820849 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = 0 . 0821$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(iii)

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \text{e}^{-0.01} = 0 . 990049 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = 0 . 990$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: P(X = 0) = 0.000912 when λ = 7, or answers which round to 0.000912. Accept $\text{e}^{-7}$.
> 
> **B1**: P(X = 0) = 0.0821 when λ = 2.5, or answers which round to 0.0821. Accept $\text{e}^{-2.5}$.

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{1}}{1!} = λ \text{e}^{-λ}$

(i)

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = 7 \text{e}^{-7} = 0 . 00638317 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = 0 . 00638$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(ii)

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = 2 . 5 \text{e}^{-2.5} = 0 . 205212 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = 0 . 205$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

(iii)

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = 0 . 01 \text{e}^{-0.01} = 0 . 00990049 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = 0 . 00990$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problemMd:
Given that $λ = k$, find a simplified expression in terms of $k$ for

(i) $\text{P} ( X = 0 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( X = 1 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Substitute $λ = k$ and $r = 0$ into $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \text{e}^{-k} \frac{k^{0}}{0!}$

Simplify using $k^{0} = 1$ and $0 ! = 1$

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \text{e}^{-k}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Substitute $λ = k$ and $r = 1$

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = \text{e}^{-k} \frac{k^{1}}{1!}$

Simplify using $k^{1} = k$ and $1 ! = 1$

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = k \text{e}^{-k}$

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is worth knowing $\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \text{e}^{-λ}$ and $\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = λ \text{e}^{-λ}$ by heart. They come up constantly, for example in "at least one" questions, where $\text{P} ( X \geq 1 ) = 1 - \text{e}^{-λ}$, and in questions that give you $\text{P} ( X = 0 )$ and ask you to find $λ$.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: P(X = 0) = $\text{e}^{-k}$.
> 
> **B1**: P(X = 1) = $k \text{e}^{-k}$. Accept $\frac{k}{\text{e}^{k}}$.

parts.problemMd:
For each of the following random variables, find the mean and the standard deviation.

(i) `X \sim \text{Po}(4)`

(ii) `X \sim \text{Po}(1)`

(iii) `X \sim \text{Po}(5.4)`
parts.solutionMd:
For `X \sim \text{Po}(\lambda)` the mean and the variance are both equal to $λ$

$μ = λ$

$σ^{2} = λ$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$σ = \sqrt{λ}$

(i)

$σ = \sqrt{4} = 2$

$μ = 4 ,  σ = 2$

**[B1]**

(ii)

$σ = \sqrt{1} = 1$

$μ = 1 ,  σ = 1$

**[B1]**

(iii)

$σ = \sqrt{5.4} = 2 . 32379 \dots$

**Final answer:** $μ = 5 . 4 ,  σ = 2 . 32$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: μ = 4 and σ = 2. Both values are needed.
> 
> **B1**: μ = 1 and σ = 1. Both values are needed.
> 
> **B1**: μ = 5.4 and σ = 2.32, or answers which round to 2.32. Accept $σ = \sqrt{5.4}$. Both values are needed.
> 
> A variance given in place of a standard deviation (for example σ = 4 in (i)) does not score.

parts.problemMd:
The random variable `X \sim \text{Po}(6.3)`.

(i) By taking out a common factor of $\text{e}^{-λ}$, factorise the expression

$\text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{4}}{4!} + \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{5}}{5!} + \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{6}}{6!} + \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{7}}{7!} + \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{8}}{8!}$

(ii) Hence calculate $\text{P} ( 4 \leq X \leq 8 )$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Every term has a factor of $\text{e}^{-λ}$, so take it outside a bracket

`\text{e}^{-\lambda}\left(\dfrac{\lambda^{4}}{4!} + \dfrac{\lambda^{5}}{5!} + \dfrac{\lambda^{6}}{6!} + \dfrac{\lambda^{7}}{7!} + \dfrac{\lambda^{8}}{8!}\right)`

**[B1]**

(ii)

$\text{P} ( 4 \leq X \leq 8 )$ is the sum of the terms for $r = 4$ to $r = 8$, which is the expression in (i), so substitute $λ = 6 . 3$

`\text{P}(4 \leq X \leq 8) = \text{e}^{-6.3}\left(\dfrac{6.3^{4}}{4!} + \dfrac{6.3^{5}}{5!} + \dfrac{6.3^{6}}{6!} + \dfrac{6.3^{7}}{7!} + \dfrac{6.3^{8}}{8!}\right)`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( 4 \leq X \leq 8 ) = 0 . 688393 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 4 \leq X \leq 8 ) = 0 . 688$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When you add several Poisson probabilities with the same $λ$, take out the common factor $\text{e}^{-λ}$ first. You then only need $\text{e}^{-λ}$ once, and the bracket is quick to type into a calculator. This saves time on every "at most", "at least" and "between" question.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A correct factorised expression with $\text{e}^{-λ}$ outside the bracket. A factorisation that also takes out $λ^{4}$ or $\frac{λ^{4}}{4!}$ is also accepted.
> 
> **M1**: λ = 6.3 substituted into the factorised expression, or the sum of the five terms for r = 4 to 8 written out.
> 
> **A1**: P(4 ≤ X ≤ 8) = 0.688, or answers which round to 0.688.
> 
> If 0.688 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for (ii).

parts.problemMd:
Calculate

(i) $\text{P} ( X \leq 3 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( 5 \leq X \leq 7 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

$X \leq 3$ means $X = 0 ,  1 ,  2 \text{or} 3$, so add those four terms of $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $λ = 6 . 3$

$\text{P} ( X \leq 3 ) = \text{e}^{-6.3} \frac{6.3^{0}}{0!} + \text{e}^{-6.3} \frac{6.3^{1}}{1!} + \text{e}^{-6.3} \frac{6.3^{2}}{2!} + \text{e}^{-6.3} \frac{6.3^{3}}{3!}$

**[M1]**

Take out the common factor $\text{e}^{-6.3}$

`\text{P}(X \leq 3) = \text{e}^{-6.3}\left(1 + 6.3 + \dfrac{6.3^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{6.3^{3}}{6}\right)`

$\text{P} ( X \leq 3 ) = 0 . 126373 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \leq 3 ) = 0 . 126$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

$5 \leq X \leq 7$ means $X = 5 ,  6 \text{or} 7$, so add those three terms

$\text{P} ( 5 \leq X \leq 7 ) = \text{e}^{-6.3} \frac{6.3^{5}}{5!} + \text{e}^{-6.3} \frac{6.3^{6}}{6!} + \text{e}^{-6.3} \frac{6.3^{7}}{7!}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( 5 \leq X \leq 7 ) = 0 . 454844 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( 5 \leq X \leq 7 ) = 0 . 455$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: P(0) + P(1) + P(2) + P(3), with all four terms correct. Accept unsimplified, or the factorised form `\text{e}^{-6.3}\left(1 + 6.3 + \dfrac{6.3^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{6.3^{3}}{6}\right)`.
> 
> **A1**: P(X ≤ 3) = 0.126, or answers which round to 0.126.
> 
> **M1**: P(5) + P(6) + P(7), with all three terms correct. Accept unsimplified, or the factorised form `\text{e}^{-6.3}\dfrac{6.3^{5}}{5!}\left(1 + \dfrac{6.3}{6} + \dfrac{6.3^{2}}{42}\right)`.
> 
> **A1**: P(5 ≤ X ≤ 7) = 0.455, or answers which round to 0.455.
> 
> If 0.126 or 0.455 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for that answer.

parts.problemMd:
A random variable `X \sim \text{Po}(6)`.

Find the exact value, in terms of $\text{e}$, of

(i) $\text{P} ( X = 3 )$

(ii) $\text{P} ( X = 4 )$

(iii) $\text{P} ( X = 5 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $λ = 6$ and $r = 3$

$\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = \text{e}^{-6} \frac{6^{3}}{3!}$

**[M1]**

Simplify the fraction, since $6^{3} = 216$ and $3 ! = 6$

$\frac{6^{3}}{3!} = \frac{216}{6} = 36$

$\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = 36 \text{e}^{-6}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Use the formula with $r = 4$

$\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \text{e}^{-6} \frac{6^{4}}{4!}$

$\frac{6^{4}}{4!} = \frac{1296}{24} = 54$

$\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = 54 \text{e}^{-6}$

**[A1]**

(iii)

Use the formula with $r = 5$

$\text{P} ( X = 5 ) = \text{e}^{-6} \frac{6^{5}}{5!}$

$\frac{6^{5}}{5!} = \frac{7776}{120} = \frac{324}{5}$

$\text{P} ( X = 5 ) = \frac{324}{5} \text{e}^{-6}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the Poisson formula with λ = 6 for any one of the three probabilities.
> 
> **A1**: P(X = 3) = $36 \text{e}^{-6}$.
> 
> **A1**: P(X = 4) = $54 \text{e}^{-6}$.
> 
> **A1**: P(X = 5) = $\frac{324}{5} \text{e}^{-6}$. Accept $64 . 8 \text{e}^{-6}$.
> 
> The answers must be exact, in terms of e. A decimal answer alone does not earn the A1 for that sub-part.

parts.problemMd:
Use your answers to part (a) to find the exact value of

(i) $\frac{6}{4} \text{P} ( X = 3 )$

(ii) $\frac{6}{5} \text{P} ( X = 4 )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Multiply the answer to (a)(i) by $\frac{6}{4}$

$\frac{6}{4} \text{P} ( X = 3 ) = \frac{6}{4} \times 36 \text{e}^{-6}$

$\frac{6}{4} \text{P} ( X = 3 ) = 54 \text{e}^{-6}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Multiply the answer to (a)(ii) by $\frac{6}{5}$

$\frac{6}{5} \text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \frac{6}{5} \times 54 \text{e}^{-6}$

$\frac{6}{5} \text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \frac{324}{5} \text{e}^{-6}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $54 \text{e}^{-6}$. Follow through $\frac{6}{4}$ times your answer to (a)(i).
> 
> **B1**: $\frac{324}{5} \text{e}^{-6}$, or $64 . 8 \text{e}^{-6}$. Follow through $\frac{6}{5}$ times your answer to (a)(ii).

parts.problemMd:
Compare your answers to part (a) and part (b), then use the pattern to write down an expression, in terms of $k$, for

$\frac{6}{k+1} \text{P} ( X = k )$

where $k$ is an integer and $k \geq 0$.
parts.solutionMd:
Comparing (a) and (b), multiplying each probability by $\frac{6}{k+1}$ gives the next probability along

$\frac{6}{4} \text{P} ( X = 3 ) = \text{P} ( X = 4 )$

$\frac{6}{5} \text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \text{P} ( X = 5 )$

So the pattern is

$\frac{6}{k+1} \text{P} ( X = k ) = \text{P} ( X = k + 1 )$

Write $\text{P} ( X = k + 1 )$ using the Poisson formula with $r = k + 1$

$\frac{6}{k+1} \text{P} ( X = k ) = \text{e}^{-6} \frac{6^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}$

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The same pattern holds for any Poisson distribution: if `X \sim \text{Po}(\lambda)`, then $\text{P} ( X = k + 1 ) = \frac{λ}{k+1} \text{P} ( X = k )$. It is a quick way to build a list of probabilities one term at a time, each from the one before.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\text{e}^{-6} \frac{6^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}$. Accept $\text{P} ( X = k + 1 )$.

parts.problemMd:
Naomi, a teacher, receives emails at a constant average rate during the school day. Naomi models the number of emails she receives within a fixed period of time using a Poisson distribution, $\text{Po} ( λ )$.

Write down two assumptions that Naomi has made about the emails in order to use a Poisson model.
parts.solutionMd:
The constant average rate is given, so state two of the other Poisson conditions (randomly, independently, singly) in context

**Final answer:** **The emails arrive independently of each other**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **The emails arrive singly, so two never arrive at exactly the same time**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: One correct assumption, in context. For example, emails arrive independently, or emails arrive singly, or emails arrive at random.
> 
> **B1**: A second, different correct assumption, in context.
> 
> "At a constant average rate" is given in the question, so it is not credited as one of the two assumptions. Two correct assumptions that are not in context (for example "events are independent") score 1 mark only.

parts.problemMd:
Naomi knows that on average she receives 10 emails in one hour.

Calculate the value of $λ$ in the case when Naomi is modelling the number of emails she receives in

(i) two hours

(ii) 15 minutes

(iii) one hour and 10 minutes.
parts.solutionMd:
The rate is constant, so scale the mean of 10 per hour to find the mean number of emails in each period

(i)

$λ = 10 \times 2$

$λ = 20$

**[B1]**

(ii)

15 minutes is $\frac{15}{60}$ of an hour

$λ = 10 \times \frac{15}{60}$

$λ = 2 . 5$

**[B1]**

(iii)

One hour and 10 minutes is 70 minutes, which is $\frac{70}{60}$ of an hour

$λ = 10 \times \frac{70}{60} = \frac{35}{3}$

**Final answer:** $λ = 11 . 7$** (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: λ = 20.
> 
> **B1**: λ = 2.5.
> 
> **B1**: λ = 11.7, or answers which round to 11.7. Accept $\frac{35}{3}$.

parts.problemMd:
The random variables `R \sim \text{Po}(2)`, `S \sim \text{Po}(3)` and `T \sim \text{Po}(4)` are independent.

Write down the distribution of

(i) $R + S$

(ii) $S + T$
parts.solutionMd:
For independent Poisson variables, add the means: if `X \sim \text{Po}(\lambda)` and `Y \sim \text{Po}(\mu)` are independent, then

`X + Y \sim \text{Po}(\lambda + \mu)`

(i)

$2 + 3 = 5$

`R + S \sim \text{Po}(5)`

**[B1]**

(ii)

$3 + 4 = 7$

`S + T \sim \text{Po}(7)`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: R + S ~ Po(5). Accept "Poisson with mean 5".
> 
> **B1**: S + T ~ Po(7). Accept "Poisson with mean 7".

parts.problemMd:
(i) Write down the distribution of $R + T$.

(ii) Find $\text{P} ( R + T = 5 )$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

$R$ and $T$ are independent Poisson variables, so add their means

$2 + 4 = 6$

`R + T \sim \text{Po}(6)`

**[B1]**

(ii)

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $λ = 6$ and $r = 5$

$\text{P} ( R + T = 5 ) = \text{e}^{-6} \frac{6^{5}}{5!}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( R + T = 5 ) = 0 . 160623 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( R + T = 5 ) = 0 . 161$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: R + T ~ Po(6). Accept "Poisson with mean 6".
> 
> **M1**: A correct expression for P(X = 5) with λ = 6, $\text{e}^{-6} \frac{6^{5}}{5!}$. Follow through your mean from (i).
> 
> **A1**: P(R + T = 5) = 0.161, or answers which round to 0.161. Accept $\frac{324}{5} \text{e}^{-6}$.
>

parts.problemMd:
The number of times that the internet connection at Amira's house disconnects during a day is denoted by $X$. On average, the internet disconnects 5 times each day.

State a suitable distribution for $X$, giving the value of any parameter, and state one assumption that is required for this model to be valid in this context.
parts.solutionMd:
The disconnections are random events with a mean of 5 per day

`X \sim \text{Po}(5)`

**[B1]**

State one of the Poisson conditions (randomly, independently, singly, at a constant average rate) in context

**Final answer:** **The internet disconnects independently, so one disconnection does not affect when the next one happens**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: X ~ Po(5). Accept "Poisson with mean 5".
> 
> **B1**: One correct assumption, in context. For example, disconnections occur independently, or at random, or singly (one at a time), or at a constant average rate. An assumption that does not mention the internet or the disconnections does not score.

parts.problemMd:
Find the probability that, during a randomly chosen day, the internet at Amira's house disconnects

(i) exactly 4 times

(ii) at most 3 times

(iii) at least 2 times.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $λ = 5$ and $r = 4$

$\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \text{e}^{-5} \frac{5^{4}}{4!}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = 0 . 175467 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = 0 . 175$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

"At most 3 times" means $X = 0 ,  1 ,  2 \text{or} 3$, so add those four terms

`\text{P}(X \leq 3) = \text{e}^{-5}\left(\dfrac{5^{0}}{0!} + \dfrac{5^{1}}{1!} + \dfrac{5^{2}}{2!} + \dfrac{5^{3}}{3!}\right)`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X \leq 3 ) = 0 . 265025 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \leq 3 ) = 0 . 265$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(iii)

"At least 2 times" is every outcome except $X = 0$ and $X = 1$, so subtract those two terms from 1

`\text{P}(X \geq 2) = 1 - \text{e}^{-5}\left(\dfrac{5^{0}}{0!} + \dfrac{5^{1}}{1!}\right)`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X \geq 2 ) = 0 . 959572 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X \geq 2 ) = 0 . 960$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A correct expression for P(X = 4), $\text{e}^{-5} \frac{5^{4}}{4!}$. Follow through your λ from (a).
> 
> **A1**: P(X = 4) = 0.175, or answers which round to 0.175.
> 
> **M1**: P(0) + P(1) + P(2) + P(3) written out with any λ. Allow one term missing or one extra term.
> 
> **A1**: P(X ≤ 3) = 0.265, or answers which round to 0.265.
> 
> **M1**: 1 − (P(0) + P(1)) written out with any λ. Allow one term missing or one extra term.
> 
> **A1**: P(X ≥ 2) = 0.960, or answers which round to 0.960.
> 
> If 0.175, 0.265 or 0.960 is given with no working, for example straight from a calculator, award 1 mark only for that answer.

parts.problemMd:
The numbers of pieces of ham and pieces of salami on a pizza from Pizza Palace have the independent distributions $\text{Po} ( 6 . 2 )$ and $\text{Po} ( 4 . 9 )$ respectively. Roberto orders a pizza from Pizza Palace.

parts.problemMd:
Roger is investigating historical data from World War II. In south London, an area of 144 km² was divided into 576 equal squares, and the number of times each square was hit by a flying bomb over a period of time was recorded. | **Number of times hit by a flying bomb** | **Number of squares** |
|---|---|
| 0 | 229 |
| 1 | 211 |
| 2 | 93 |
| 3 | 35 |
| 4 | 7 |
| 5 or more | 1 |

Roger suggests that a Poisson distribution with mean $\frac{537}{576}$ would be an appropriate model for the number of times a square was hit by a flying bomb.

(i) By finding probabilities using Roger's model, estimate the expected number of squares that would be hit, respectively, by 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 or more flying bombs.

(ii) By comparing the actual number of squares in the table with the expected numbers of squares from part (i), state whether Roger's model is appropriate.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Let $X$ be the number of hits on a square

`X \sim \text{Po}\left(\dfrac{537}{576}\right)`

$\text{P} ( X = 0 ) = \text{e}^{-λ} = 0 . 393650 \dots$

$\text{P} ( X = 1 ) = \text{e}^{-λ} λ = 0 . 366997 \dots$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 2 ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{2}}{2!} = 0 . 171074 \dots$

$\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{3}}{3!} = 0 . 0531636 \dots$

$\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{4}}{4!} = 0 . 0123910 \dots$

**[A1]**

"5 or more" is every outcome not already counted, so subtract the sum of the others from 1

`\text{P}(X \geq 5) = 1 - \left(\text{P}(X = 0) + \text{P}(X = 1) + \text{P}(X = 2) + \text{P}(X = 3) + \text{P}(X = 4)\right) = 0.00272335\ldots`

**[B1]**

The expected number of squares for each value is 576 times its probability

$576 \times 0 . 393650 \dots = 226 . 74 \dots$

Do the same for each row

| **Number of hits** | **Probability** | **Expected number of squares** | **Actual number of squares** |
|---|---|---|---|

| 3 | 0.0532 | **Final answer:** **30.6** | 35 |
| 4 | 0.0124 | **Final answer:** **7.1** | 7 |
| 5 or more | 0.0027 | **Final answer:** **1.6** | 1 |

**[A1]**

(ii)

Compare the expected and actual numbers row by row: they are very close in every row (for example 211.4 and 211 for one hit, 7.1 and 7 for four hits)

**Final answer:** **The expected numbers are very close to the actual numbers, so Roger's model is appropriate**

parts.problemMd:
$X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are random variables with `X \sim \text{Po}(\alpha)`, `Y \sim \text{Po}(\beta)` and `Z \sim \text{Po}(\gamma)`.

(i) Given that $\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = \text{P} ( X = 7 )$, find the value of $α$.

(ii) Given that $\text{P} ( Y = 0 ) = 0 . 253$, find the value of $β$.

(iii) Given that `5\text{Var}(Z) = \left(\text{E}(Z)\right)^{2} - 6`, find the value of $γ$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ for each side

$\text{e}^{-α} \frac{α^{3}}{3!} = \text{e}^{-α} \frac{α^{7}}{7!}$

Divide both sides by $\text{e}^{-α} α^{3}$, which is not zero

$\frac{1}{3!} = \frac{α^{4}}{7!}$

**[M1]**

Multiply both sides by $7 !$

$α^{4} = \frac{7!}{3!} = 4 \times 5 \times 6 \times 7 = 840$

**[M1]**

$α$ is a mean, so take the positive fourth root

`\alpha = \sqrt[4]{840} = 5.38356\ldots`

**Final answer:** $α = 5 . 38$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

Use the formula with $r = 0$; since $β^{0} = 1$ and $0 ! = 1$, this is $\text{e}^{-β}$

$\text{e}^{-β} = 0 . 253$

Take natural logarithms of both sides

`-\beta = \text{ln}\left(0.253\right)`

**[M1]**

`\beta = -\text{ln}\left(0.253\right) = 1.37436\ldots`

**Final answer:** $β = 1 . 37$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(iii)

For a Poisson distribution the mean and the variance are both equal to the parameter

$\text{E} ( Z ) = \text{Var} ( Z ) = γ$

Substitute into the given equation

$5 γ = γ^{2} - 6$

Rearrange to a quadratic equal to zero

$γ^{2} - 5 γ - 6 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise

$( γ - 6 ) ( γ + 1 ) = 0$

$γ = 6$* or *$γ = - 1$

$γ$ is the mean of a Poisson distribution, so it must be positive; reject $γ = - 1$

$γ = 6$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Equating the two Poisson expressions and cancelling $\text{e}^{-α}$ to reach an equation in α only.
> 
> **M1**: $α^{4} = 840$, or $α^{4} = \frac{7!}{3!}$.
> 
> **A1**: α = 5.38, or answers which round to 5.38. Accept `\sqrt[4]{840}`.
> 
> **M1**: $\text{e}^{-β} = 0 . 253$ with logarithms taken, `-\beta = \text{ln}\left(0.253\right)` or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: β = 1.37, or answers which round to 1.37. Accept `\text{ln}\left(\dfrac{1000}{253}\right)`.
> 
> **M1**: Using E(Z) = Var(Z) = γ to form a correct quadratic, $γ^{2} - 5 γ - 6 = 0$ or equivalent.

In a computer game, enemies appear at random and at a constant average rate of 2.5 per minute. You may assume that enemies appear independently of one another.

Find the probability that exactly 10 enemies appear during a randomly chosen 5-minute period.
parts.solutionMd:
Multiply the rate per minute by 5 to find the mean number of enemies in 5 minutes

$λ = 2 . 5 \times 5 = 12 . 5$

**[B1]**

Let $X$ be the number of enemies in 5 minutes

`X \sim \text{Po}(12.5)`

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $r = 10$

$\text{P} ( X = 10 ) = \text{e}^{-12.5} \frac{12.5^{10}}{10!}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( X = 10 ) = 0 . 0956436 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( X = 10 ) = 0 . 0956$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the probability that at least 3 enemies appear during a randomly chosen 90-second period.

**[B1]**

Let $Y$ be the number of enemies in 90 seconds

`Y \sim \text{Po}(3.75)`

"At least 3" is every outcome except 0, 1 and 2, so subtract those three terms from 1

`\text{P}(Y \geq 3) = 1 - \text{e}^{-3.75}\left(1 + 3.75 + \dfrac{3.75^{2}}{2!}\right)`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( Y \geq 3 ) = 0 . 722931 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( Y \geq 3 ) = 0 . 723$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: λ = 3.75 for 90 seconds, seen or implied.

parts.problemMd:
The probability that at least one enemy appears during a $k$-minute period is 0.999.

Find the value of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
The mean in $k$ minutes is $2 . 5 k$, and "at least one" is every outcome except none

$1 - \text{e}^{-2.5k} = 0 . 999$

**[M1]**

Rearrange to make the exponential the subject

$\text{e}^{-2.5k} = 0 . 001$

Take natural logarithms of both sides

`-2.5k = \text{ln}\left(0.001\right)`

**[M1]**

Divide by $- 2 . 5$

`k = \dfrac{\text{ln}\left(0.001\right)}{-2.5} = 2.763102\ldots`

**Final answer:** $k = 2 . 76$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $1 - \text{e}^{-2.5k} = 0 . 999$, or $\text{e}^{-λ} = 0 . 001$ with λ = 2.5k. Condone an inequality sign in place of "=".
> 
> **M1**: Logarithms taken correctly, `-2.5k = \text{ln}\left(0.001\right)` or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: k = 2.76, or answers which round to 2.76. Accept `\dfrac{6}{5}\,\text{ln}\left(10\right)` or `\dfrac{\text{ln}\left(1000\right)}{2.5}`.

parts.problemMd:

Stating a necessary assumption, find the probability that Matt receives fewer than 4 messages from Danny during a randomly chosen 2-hour period.
parts.solutionMd:
State one of the Poisson conditions (randomly, independently, singly, at a constant average rate) in context

**Final answer:** **Danny's messages arrive independently of each other**

**[B1]**

The mean for 2 hours is twice the hourly mean

$λ = 1 . 7 \times 2 = 3 . 4$

**[B1]**

Let $D$ be the number of messages from Danny in 2 hours

`D \sim \text{Po}(3.4)`

"Fewer than 4" means $D = 0 ,  1 ,  2 \text{or} 3$

`\text{P}(D < 4) = \text{e}^{-3.4}\left(1 + 3.4 + \dfrac{3.4^{2}}{2!} + \dfrac{3.4^{3}}{3!}\right)`

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( D < 4 ) = 0 . 558357 \dots$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Stating a further assumption needed, find the probability that Matt receives exactly 6 messages in total during a randomly chosen 1-hour period.
parts.solutionMd:
The means can only be added if the three numbers of messages are independent of each other

**Final answer:** **Danny, Jessica and Luke send their messages independently of each other**

**[B1]**

The sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson, with the means added

$λ = 1 . 7 + 1 . 5 + 1 . 1 = 4 . 3$

Let $T$ be the total number of messages in 1 hour

`T \sim \text{Po}(4.3)`

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( T = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $r = 6$

$\text{P} ( T = 6 ) = \text{e}^{-4.3} \frac{4.3^{6}}{6!}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( T = 6 ) = 0 . 119127 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( T = 6 ) = 0 . 119$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The messages from the three friends are independent of each other (in context).
> 
> **M1**: A correct expression for P(T = 6) using the combined mean, λ = 1.7 + 1.5 + 1.1. Adding probabilities instead of means scores M0.

parts.problemMd: Find the probability that Matt receives at least one message from any of the three friends during a randomly chosen 1-hour period.
parts.solutionMd:
"At least one message in total" is every outcome of $T$ except $T = 0$

$\text{P} ( T \geq 1 ) = 1 - \text{e}^{-4.3}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( T \geq 1 ) = 0 . 986431 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( T \geq 1 ) = 0 . 986$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **A1**: 0.986, or answers which round to 0.986.

parts.problemMd: Find the probability that Matt receives at least one message from each friend during a randomly chosen 1-hour period.
parts.solutionMd:
For each friend, use $1 - \text{e}^{-λ}$ with that friend's hourly mean

$\text{P} ( \text{at least one from Danny} ) = 1 - \text{e}^{-1.7}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( \text{at least one from Jessica} ) = 1 - \text{e}^{-1.5}$

$\text{P} ( \text{at least one from Luke} ) = 1 - \text{e}^{-1.1}$

The three friends are independent, so multiply the three probabilities

`\left(1 - \text{e}^{-1.7}\right)\left(1 - \text{e}^{-1.5}\right)\left(1 - \text{e}^{-1.1}\right)`

**[M1]**

$= 0 . 423592 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( \text{at least one from each} ) = 0 . 424$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not use the total from part (b) here. Three messages in total could all come from Danny, so $\text{P} ( T \geq 3 )$ is not the same as one message from each friend. When a question says "from each", work with each person's own distribution and multiply.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $1 - \text{e}^{-λ}$ for at least one of the friends, with that friend's mean.
> 
> **M1**: The product of three probabilities, each of the form $1 - \text{e}^{-λ}$.

parts.problemMd:

State two conditions necessary for a Poisson distribution to be a suitable model for the number of times that the smoke detector rings.
parts.solutionMd:
State two of the Poisson conditions (randomly, independently, singly, at a constant average rate) in context

**Final answer:** **The smoke detector rings at random and independently, so one ring does not affect when the next happens**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **The smoke detector rings at a constant average rate throughout the day**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: One correct condition, in context. For example, the rings occur independently, or at random, or singly (one at a time), or at a constant average rate.

parts.problemMd:
Assume now that a Poisson distribution is a suitable model.

(i) Find the probability that the smoke detector rings exactly 3 times on each day of a randomly chosen 4-day period.

(ii) Find the probability that the smoke detector rings exactly 12 times during a randomly chosen 4-day period.

(iii) Explain why the answers to part (b)(i) and part (b)(ii) are different.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Let $X$ be the number of rings in a day

`X \sim \text{Po}(5)`

Find the probability of exactly 3 rings on one day

$\text{P} ( X = 3 ) = \text{e}^{-5} \frac{5^{3}}{3!} = 0 . 140373 \dots$

The 4 days are independent, so multiply this probability 4 times

`\left(\text{e}^{-5}\dfrac{5^{3}}{3!}\right)^{4}`

**[M1]**

$= 0 . 000388280 \dots$

**Final answer:** $0 . 000388$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

The mean for 4 days is 4 times the daily mean

$λ = 5 \times 4 = 20$

**[B1]**

Let $Y$ be the number of rings in 4 days

`Y \sim \text{Po}(20)`

To find the probability, use $\text{P} ( Y = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$ with $r = 12$

$\text{P} ( Y = 12 ) = \text{e}^{-20} \frac{20^{12}}{12!}$

**[M1]**

$\text{P} ( Y = 12 ) = 0 . 0176251 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( Y = 12 ) = 0 . 0176$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(iii)

Compare which outcomes each part counts

**Final answer:** **In (i) the 12 rings must be split as 3, 3, 3, 3, which is only one of the many ways of getting 12 rings in 4 days (for example 12, 0, 0, 0 or 5, 4, 2, 1), so (i) is part of (ii) and its probability is smaller**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: `\left(\text{P}(X = 3)\right)^{4}` with P(X = 3) from Po(5) written as an expression. Allow any λ.
> 
> **A1**: 0.000388, or answers which round to 0.000388. Accept $3 . 88 \times 10^{-4}$.
> 
> **B1**: λ = 20 for 4 days, seen or implied.
> 
> **M1**: A correct expression for P(Y = 12) with any λ.
> 
> **A1**: 0.0176, or answers which round to 0.0176.
> 
> **B1**: (i) is only one particular way of getting a total of 12 rings, while (ii) includes every way of getting a total of 12. Accept "(i) is a subset of (ii)" or an example of another split. "One is per day and one is in total" alone does not score.

parts.problemMd: Given that the smoke detector rings at least once during a randomly chosen 6-hour period, find the probability that it rings no more than 4 times during this period.
parts.solutionMd:
6 hours is $\frac{6}{24}$ of a day, so scale the daily mean to find the mean number of rings in 6 hours

$λ = 5 \times \frac{6}{24} = 1 . 25$

**[B1]**

Let $W$ be the number of rings in 6 hours

`W \sim \text{Po}(1.25)`

Use the conditional probability formula

`\text{P}(W \leq 4 \mid W \geq 1) = \dfrac{\text{P}(W \leq 4 \text{ and } W \geq 1)}{\text{P}(W \geq 1)} = \dfrac{\text{P}(1 \leq W \leq 4)}{\text{P}(W \geq 1)}`

Find the numerator: $W = 1 ,  2 ,  3 \text{or} 4$

`\text{P}(1 \leq W \leq 4) = \text{e}^{-1.25}\left(1.25 + \dfrac{1.25^{2}}{2!} + \dfrac{1.25^{3}}{3!} + \dfrac{1.25^{4}}{4!}\right) = 0.704370\ldots`

**[M1]**

Find the denominator, then divide

$\text{P} ( W \geq 1 ) = 1 - \text{e}^{-1.25} = 0 . 713495 \dots$

`\text{P}(W \leq 4 \mid W \geq 1) = \dfrac{0.704370\ldots}{0.713495\ldots}`

**[M1]**

$= 0 . 987211 \dots$

**Final answer:** `\text{P}(W \leq 4 \mid W \geq 1) = 0.987`** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: λ = 1.25 for 6 hours, seen or implied.
> 
> **M1**: P(1) + P(2) + P(3) + P(4) written out with any λ, or P(W ≤ 4) − P(W = 0). Allow one term missing or one extra term.
> 
> **M1**: The numerator divided by P(W ≥ 1) = $1 - \text{e}^{-λ}$.
> 
> **A1**: 0.987, or answers which round to 0.987.
> 
> Using P(W ≤ 4) (including W = 0) as the numerator scores the second M1 but not the A1.

parts.problemMd:
The random variables `X \sim \text{Po}(\alpha)`, `Y \sim \text{Po}(\beta)` and `Z \sim \text{Po}(\gamma)`.

(i) Given that $\text{P} ( X = 4 ) = \text{P} ( X = 2 ) + \text{P} ( X = 3 )$, find the value of $α$.

(ii) Given that $\text{P} ( Y \geq 1 ) = 0 . 314$, find the value of $β$.

(iii) Given that $\text{P} ( Z = k + 1 ) = \text{P} ( Z = k - 1 )$ where $k$ is a positive integer, find an expression for $γ$ in terms of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Write each probability using $\text{P} ( X = r ) = \text{e}^{-λ} \frac{λ^{r}}{r!}$

$\text{e}^{-α} \frac{α^{4}}{4!} = \text{e}^{-α} \frac{α^{2}}{2!} + \text{e}^{-α} \frac{α^{3}}{3!}$

Divide every term by $\text{e}^{-α} α^{2}$, which is not zero

$\frac{α^{2}}{24} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{α}{6}$

**[M1]**

Multiply by 24 and rearrange to a quadratic equal to zero

$α^{2} - 4 α - 12 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise

$( α - 6 ) ( α + 2 ) = 0$

$α = 6$* or *$α = - 2$

$α$ is the mean of a Poisson distribution, so it must be positive; reject $α = - 2$

$α = 6$

**[A1]**

(ii)

"At least 1" is every outcome except $Y = 0$

$1 - \text{e}^{-β} = 0 . 314$

$\text{e}^{-β} = 0 . 686$

Take natural logarithms of both sides

`-\beta = \text{ln}\left(0.686\right)`

**[M1]**

`\beta = -\text{ln}\left(0.686\right) = 0.376877\ldots`

**Final answer:** $β = 0 . 377$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(iii)

Write each probability using the Poisson formula

$\text{e}^{-γ} \frac{γ^{k+1}}{(k+1)!} = \text{e}^{-γ} \frac{γ^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}$

Divide both sides by $\text{e}^{-γ} γ^{k-1}$, which is not zero

$\frac{γ^{2}}{(k+1)!} = \frac{1}{(k-1)!}$

Multiply both sides by $( k + 1 ) !$, using $( k + 1 ) ! = ( k + 1 ) \times k \times ( k - 1 ) !$

$γ^{2} = \frac{(k+1)!}{(k-1)!} = k ( k + 1 )$

**[M1]**

$γ$ is a mean, so take the positive square root

$γ = \sqrt{k(k+1)}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Equating the Poisson expressions and cancelling $\text{e}^{-α}$ to reach an equation in α only.
> 
> **M1**: A correct three-term quadratic, $α^{2} - 4 α - 12 = 0$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: α = 6 only, with −2 rejected.
> 
> **M1**: $\text{e}^{-β} = 0 . 686$ with logarithms taken, `-\beta = \text{ln}\left(0.686\right)` or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: β = 0.377, or answers which round to 0.377. Accept `\text{ln}\left(\dfrac{500}{343}\right)`.
> 
> **M1**: $γ^{2} = k ( k + 1 )$, or $γ^{2} = \frac{(k+1)!}{(k-1)!}$.
> 
> **A1**: $γ = \sqrt{k(k+1)}$ or $\sqrt{k^{2}+k}$. A ± answer does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
The number of mistakes made by a student, Priya, in a 20-minute revision period is modelled by the distribution $\text{Po} ( 1 . 2 )$. The number of mistakes made by a different student, Qays, in a 30-minute revision period is modelled by the distribution $\text{Po} ( 2 . 2 )$.

Stating a necessary assumption, find the probability that, in a randomly chosen 1-hour revision period, Priya makes exactly 2 mistakes and Qays makes exactly 1 mistake. Give your answer in the form $\frac{a}{b} \text{e}^{c}$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
The two probabilities can only be multiplied if the two students' mistakes are independent

**Final answer:** **Priya and Qays make their mistakes independently of each other**

**[B1]**

Scale each mean to 1 hour: three 20-minute periods for Priya, two 30-minute periods for Qays

$λ_{P} = 1 . 2 \times 3 = 3 . 6$

$λ_{Q} = 2 . 2 \times 2 = 4 . 4$

**[B1]**

With `X \sim \text{Po}(3.6)` and `Y \sim \text{Po}(4.4)` the numbers of mistakes in an hour, multiply the two Poisson probabilities

$\text{P} ( X = 2 ) \times \text{P} ( Y = 1 ) = \text{e}^{-3.6} \frac{3.6^{2}}{2!} \times \text{e}^{-4.4} \frac{4.4^{1}}{1!}$

**[M1]**

Combine the exponentials, $\text{e}^{-3.6} \times \text{e}^{-4.4} = \text{e}^{-8}$, and write $3 . 6 = \frac{18}{5}$ and $4 . 4 = \frac{22}{5}$

`= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{18}{5}\right)^{2} \times \dfrac{22}{5} \times \text{e}^{-8}`

$= \frac{324}{50} \times \frac{22}{5} \times \text{e}^{-8}$

$\frac{3564}{125} \text{e}^{-8}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The numbers of mistakes made by Priya and Qays are independent (in context).
> 
> **B1**: Both hourly means, 3.6 and 4.4, seen or implied.
> 
> **M1**: The product of two Poisson expressions, P(X = 2) × P(Y = 1), with any λ.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{3564}{125} \text{e}^{-8}$, or a = 3564, b = 125, c = −8. Accept an equivalent integer fraction such as $\frac{7128}{250} \text{e}^{-8}$. A decimal coefficient (28.512) or a decimal answer (0.00956) does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Given that Priya and Qays make a total of exactly 9 mistakes in a randomly chosen 1-hour revision period, find the probability that Priya makes exactly 5 mistakes.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the conditional probability formula. If the total is 9 and Priya makes 5, then Qays makes 4

`\text{P}(X = 5 \mid X + Y = 9) = \dfrac{\text{P}(X = 5 \text{ and } Y = 4)}{\text{P}(X + Y = 9)}`

Find the numerator, using independence

$\text{P} ( X = 5 ) \times \text{P} ( Y = 4 ) = \text{e}^{-3.6} \frac{3.6^{5}}{5!} \times \text{e}^{-4.4} \frac{4.4^{4}}{4!} = 0 . 0263982 \dots$

**[M1]**

The sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson with the means added, so `X + Y \sim \text{Po}(8)`

$\text{P} ( X + Y = 9 ) = \text{e}^{-8} \frac{8^{9}}{9!} = 0 . 124076 \dots$

**[M1]**

Divide

`\text{P}(X = 5 \mid X + Y = 9) = \dfrac{0.0263982\ldots}{0.124076\ldots}`

**[M1]**

$= 0 . 212757 \dots$

**Final answer:** `\text{P}(X = 5 \mid X + Y = 9) = 0.213`** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: P(X = 5) × P(Y = 4) written as Poisson expressions, with any λ.
> 
> **M1**: P(X + Y = 9) using the combined mean 8.
> 
> **M1**: The numerator divided by P(X + Y = 9). Cancelling the exponentials first, $\frac{\frac{3.6^{5}}{5!}\times\frac{4.4^{4}}{4!}}{\frac{8^{9}}{9!}}$, scores all three method marks.
> 
> **A1**: 0.213, or answers which round to 0.213.
> 
> Alternative method: X given X + Y = 9 is B(9, 0.45), since 3.6 ÷ 8 = 0.45; `{}^{9}C_{5}(0.45)^{5}(0.55)^{4}` scores M1 M1 M1, then A1 for 0.213.

parts.problemMd: Given instead that Priya makes exactly 5 mistakes in a randomly chosen 1-hour revision period, find the probability that Priya and Qays make a total of exactly 9 mistakes in that period.
parts.solutionMd:
If Priya makes 5 and the total is 9, then Qays makes 4. Use the conditional probability formula

`\text{P}(X + Y = 9 \mid X = 5) = \dfrac{\text{P}(X = 5 \text{ and } Y = 4)}{\text{P}(X = 5)} = \dfrac{\text{P}(X = 5) \times \text{P}(Y = 4)}{\text{P}(X = 5)}`

$\text{P} ( X = 5 )$ cancels, because $X$ and $Y$ are independent

`\text{P}(X + Y = 9 \mid X = 5) = \text{P}(Y = 4) = \text{e}^{-4.4}\dfrac{4.4^{4}}{4!}`

**[M1]**

$= 0 . 191736 \dots$

**Final answer:** `\text{P}(X + Y = 9 \mid X = 5) = 0.192`** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Recognising that the probability is P(Y = 4), written as a Poisson expression with λ = 4.4, or the ratio P(X = 5 and Y = 4) ÷ P(X = 5).
> 
> **A1**: 0.192, or answers which round to 0.192.

parts.problemMd:
In the week before a test, Priya has ten 30-minute revision periods.

Estimate the number of these revision periods during which Priya makes at least one mistake.
parts.solutionMd:
30 minutes is 1.5 twenty-minute periods, so scale Priya's mean to find her mean number of mistakes in 30 minutes

$λ = 1 . 2 \times 1 . 5 = 1 . 8$

**[B1]**

With `W \sim \text{Po}(1.8)` her number of mistakes in 30 minutes, the expected number of periods is 10 times $\text{P} ( W \geq 1 )$

`10 \times \text{P}(W \geq 1) = 10 \times \left(1 - \text{e}^{-1.8}\right)`

**[M1]**

$= 10 \times 0 . 834701 \dots = 8 . 347 \dots$

A number of revision periods is a whole number

**Final answer:** **8 revision periods**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: λ = 1.8 for 30 minutes, seen or implied.
> 
> **M1**: 10 × (1 − e^−λ), with any λ.
> 
> **A1**: 8 revision periods. Accept 8.35 seen in the working followed by 8. A decimal final answer, or "about 8", does not score. Using P(W = 1) (exactly one mistake) scores M0.

parts.problemMd:
Spelling mistakes in essays written by Gamu occur at random and at a constant average rate of 7 per 150 words. Gamu models the number of spelling mistakes using a Poisson distribution.

Find the largest number of words that Gamu can write so that the probability that she makes at least one spelling mistake does not exceed 0.75.
parts.solutionMd:
The rate is constant, so in $n$ words the mean number of mistakes is

$λ = \frac{7n}{150}$

**[B1]**

"At least one mistake" is every outcome except none, so its probability is $1 - \text{e}^{-λ}$; this must not exceed 0.75

$1 - \text{e}^{-\frac{7n}{150}} \leq 0 . 75$

**[M1]**

Rearrange to make the exponential the subject

$\text{e}^{-\frac{7n}{150}} \geq 0 . 25$

Take natural logarithms of both sides

`-\dfrac{7n}{150} \geq \text{ln}\left(0.25\right)`

**[M1]**

Multiply by $- \frac{150}{7}$, which reverses the inequality

`n \leq -\dfrac{150}{7}\,\text{ln}\left(0.25\right) = 29.706\ldots`

$n$ is a whole number of words, so take the largest whole number below 29.706

**Final answer:** **29 words**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: λ = $\frac{7n}{150}$, seen or implied.
>

Gamu writes three short essays, containing 100 words, 200 words and 250 words. An essay is returned by her lecturer if more than 1% of its words contain spelling mistakes.

You should assume that each spelling mistake is in a different word, and that the numbers of spelling mistakes in the three essays are independent.

Find the probability that all three essays are returned.
parts.solutionMd:
Find the mean number of mistakes in each essay, using 7 per 150 words

$λ_{1} = \frac{7\times100}{150} = \frac{14}{3}$

$λ_{2} = \frac{7\times200}{150} = \frac{28}{3}$

$λ_{3} = \frac{7\times250}{150} = \frac{35}{3}$

**[B1]**

1% of 100, 200 and 250 words is 1, 2 and 2.5. The number of mistakes is a whole number, so "more than 1, 2 and 2.5" means at least 2, 3 and 3. Let $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be the numbers of mistakes in the three essays

$X \geq 2$*, *$Y \geq 3$* and *$Z \geq 3$

**[B1]**

Each probability is 1 minus the terms below the threshold

`\text{P}(X \geq 2) = 1 - \text{e}^{-\frac{14}{3}}\left(1 + \dfrac{14}{3}\right) = 0.946713\ldots`

**[M1]**

`\text{P}(Y \geq 3) = 1 - \text{e}^{-\frac{28}{3}}\left(1 + \dfrac{28}{3} + \dfrac{\left(\frac{28}{3}\right)^{2}}{2!}\right) = 0.995234\ldots`

`\text{P}(Z \geq 3) = 1 - \text{e}^{-\frac{35}{3}}\left(1 + \dfrac{35}{3} + \dfrac{\left(\frac{35}{3}\right)^{2}}{2!}\right) = 0.999307\ldots`

**[A1]**

The essays are independent, so multiply the three probabilities

$0 . 946713 \dots \times 0 . 995234 \dots \times 0 . 999307 \dots$

**[M1]**

$= 0 . 941549 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{P} ( \text{all three returned} ) = 0 . 942$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: All three means, $\frac{14}{3}$, $\frac{28}{3}$ and $\frac{35}{3}$, seen or implied. Accept 4.67, 9.33 and 11.7 or better.
> 
> **B1**: The thresholds X ≥ 2, Y ≥ 3 and Z ≥ 3, seen or implied. In particular, more than 2.5 mistakes means at least 3.
> 
> **M1**: At least one tail probability written out as 1 minus Poisson terms, with any λ. Allow one term missing or one extra term.
> 
> **A1**: All three tail probabilities correct: 0.947, 0.995 and 0.999 (or better).
> 
> **M1**: The product of the three tail probabilities.
> 
> **A1**: 0.942, or answers which round to 0.942.

parts.problemMd:
For each scenario below, state, giving a reason, whether it could lead to bias in the data collected.

(i) In a survey of adults' health, a sample of people aged 70 or over is used.

(ii) To find out how much time students spend on homework each week, a teacher asks the students who attend the after-school homework club.

(iii) Randomly sampling 20 people from a population of 100 by assigning each person in the population a unique two-digit number (00-99) and then selecting 20 using a two-digit random number generator.
parts.solutionMd:
A sample is biased if some members of the population are more likely to be chosen than others, so that the sample does not represent the population

(i)

**Final answer:** **Yes, because people aged 70 or over are more likely to be in poorer health than younger adults, so the sample does not represent all adults**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **Yes, because students who go to a homework club are likely to spend more time on homework than other students**

**[B1]**

(iii)

**Final answer:** **No, because each person has their own number from 00 to 99, so every person has an equal chance of being selected**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Could lead to bias, with a reason in context, e.g. older people tend to have poorer health, or younger adults are excluded from a survey of all adults.
> 
> **B1**: Could lead to bias, with a reason in context, e.g. students at the homework club are likely to do more homework than average, or students who do not attend have no chance of being chosen.
> 
> **B1**: Would not lead to bias, because every person has an equal chance of being selected (the numbers 00 to 99 match the 100 people exactly).
> 
> Each mark needs both the decision and a reason. "Biased", "not random" or "not representative" on its own does not score.
